newsitem.title: USA: Glickman's farm law, USDA wish list languishes.
newsitem.headline: Glickman's farm law, USDA wish list languishes.

text.p: Congress was halfway through its work year with little sign it would make any of the changes in the nation's farm programme or Agriculture Department structure asked by the Clinton administration.
Action was more likely on reorganization of agricultural research programmes and updating the law that governs futures markets, analysts and congressional staff members said Wednesday.

Despite making its wishes public last winter, the administration has yet to submit legislation to implement them. Agriculture Department spokesman Jim Petterson said a legislative package containing the proposals was "within internal administration clearance."
"I would say, no, it's not a slow start to the process," said Petterson.

Changes would include a six-month extension on crop loans, making revenue insurance available nationwide, charging $390 million in meat inspection fees, federalising the department's county-level workers and putting federally appointed members on the committees that oversee local offices. The administration also has raised the idea of closing 500 more local offices.
"My view is, if you haven't sent it up (to Congress) by now, you're probably not that serious about it," said private consultant Bill Lesher.

A House Agriculture Committee staff worker said the so-called safety net proposals -- revenue insurance and longer crop loans during times of market disruption -- would require budgetary offsets elsewhere and thus were unlikely to pass. The meat inspection fee was a timeworn idea with no support, said the aide, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The chairmen of the House and Senate Agriculture committees have given a cold shoulder to longer terms for crop loans.

Glickman has taken a personal interest in federalising the county-level staff and putting appointed members on the locally elected county committees -- both as steps to combat bias against minority farmers -- but has had limited time to champion the ideas with lawmakers.

During President Clinton's first term, Congress rejected the idea of appointive members on the county committees. Lawmakers and many farmers view the county committees as a local bulwark against bureaucracy and are loath to alter them.
Since late 1994, the Agriculture Department has closed or moved 1,300 of its local offices, reducing the total to 2,500. Glickman has pledged to consult lawmakers before further cuts.
One consultant, who asked not to be named, said the House and Senage agriculture committees might do no more this year than update the Commodity Exchange Act governing the futures industry.

Major issues were whether to create professionals-only markets for sophisticated investors and clarifying the 1974 Treasury amendment intended to exempt interbank dealing from control by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The Supreme Court recently ruled the exemption applied to virtually anyone.

Senate Agriculture Committee chairman Richard Lugar has said he wants to bring fundamental reform to agricultural research, where the federal goverment spends more than $1 billion a year. Bills to reauthorize research spending were being drafted in the House and Senate.

"Research will get done. It needs to happen," said a spokesman for Lugar, an Indiana Republican. Authority for the work expires this year and some sources said a short-term extension was possible if legislation bogged down.
